# riSCC: A personalized risk model for the development of poor outcomes in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma

## Abstract

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is a prevalent disease for which improved risk stratification strategies are needed.

To develop a novel prognostic model (herein “riSCC”) for CSCC and compare riSCC performance to Brigham and Women’s Hospital and American Joint Committee on Cancer Staging eighth edition T staging systems.

Retrospective 12-center, multinational cohort study of CSCCs from 1991 to 2023. Clinical and pathologic risk factors, treatments, and outcomes were collected. Fine-Gray model was employed for each outcome with inverse probability of treatment weighting. A final model was trained for prospective use and estimation of hazard ratios.

Twenty-three thousand one hundred sixty-six localized CSCC tumors were included. riSCC prognostic model performed superiorly to American Joint Committee on Cancer eighth edition and Brigham and Women’s Hospital T staging for all outcomes. At 5 years, the C-index for riSCC ranged from 0.74 for local recurrence to 0.87 for disease specific death.

Retrospective study design.

riSCC prognostic model offers fine-grained risk estimates and improved stratification for important CSCC outcomes compared to T staging systems.

## INTRODUCTION

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is the second most common cancer worldwide. While most CSCCs are cured with surgical removal, approximately 4% will develop a nodal metastasis (NM), and 1% will disease specific death (DSD) from CSCC.1,2 Additional poor outcomes for CSCC include local recurrence (LR), distant metastasis (DM), and in-transit metastasis (ITM); however, data on the frequency of these outcomes are limited. Although the percentage of tumors that develop poor outcomes is small, given the large number of newly diagnosed CSCCs, the annual mortality likely exceeds that of malignant melanoma.3

Prognostication is essential to CSCC management, as offering treatment and surveillance intensification to all newly diagnosed cases is neither feasible nor cost-effective. The most commonly used tools for prognostication are the Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH) T Staging System and the American Joint Committee on Cancer Staging System eighth edition (AJCC8) (Table I). While both systems are based on several histologic risk factors, they do not account for important patient characteristics or treatment. Prior studies have reported limitations in the prognostic performance of these staging systems, likely due to the lack of fine-grained risk estimation.4 More recently, a personalized prognostic model for CSCC metastasis was developed based on a nationwide cohort from the Netherlands and validated on a nationwide cohort from the United Kingdom.5 This important work demonstrated the promising performance of individualized risk prediction models but evaluated only metastasis and did not include other clinically relevant CSCC outcomes.6

The purpose of this study was to develop a prognostic model for all relevant CSCC outcomes (herein called “riSCC”) based on clinical and histologic characteristics, as well as surgical treatment using an international multicenter cohort of CSCC cases.

## METHODS

### Development of cohort and data collection

The riSCC Working Group includes 12 centers: 10 in the United States (9 academic, 1 private practice), 1 in Spain (academic), and 1 in Brazil (1 public-private) that contributed CSCC data between October 1, 1991 to July 19, 2023 (Supplementary Table I, available via Mendeley at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/p7jrtfdz4g/1). Each site obtained ethics approval from its Institutional Review Board, independently reviewed patient charts, and collected data on patient and tumor information, treatments, and clinical outcomes. In situ, or basosquamous tumors and SCC of non-cutaneous origin were excluded.

The following variables were collected from the patient’s medical record: age, sex, immune status (reasons for immunosuppression, including hematologic malignancy, solid organ transplant, autoimmune disease, and/or iatrogenic immunosuppression), recurrent tumor status, anatomic location, histologic differentiation (well, moderate, or poor), perineural invasion (PNI), lymphovascular invasion (LVI), preoperative tumor diameter (in millimeters (mm), as a continuous variable), depth of invasion (tissue level depth or depth in mm), surgical treatment (wide local excision (WLE) or Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS)), margin status, and use of adjuvant therapy (including type, dose, and number of fractions for radiotherapy or chemotherapy utilized).

The date of diagnosis was defined as the date of biopsy or, if unavailable, the date of treatment (eg, surgery). Follow-up began on the date of primary treatment initiation or on the biopsy date if no treatment was performed. Clinical outcomes of interest included LR, ITM, NM, DM, and DSD, which were assigned to the primary tumor according to guidelines outlined by an expert panel on standardizing CSCC outcome reporting7: LR, tumor with comparable histology arising within the surgical scar; ITM, satellite tumors or dermal/subcutaneous metastatic deposits clinically distinct from the primary tumor and occur before the first echelon draining regional lymph nodes; NM, tumor present in the regional lymph nodes, including parotid metastases; DM, tumor involvement beyond the regional lymph nodes; and DSD, death due to CSCC or its treatment. Date of recurrence was defined as the date of histologic confirmation of CSCC outcome during follow-up. End of follow-up was the date of the last office visit by dermatology, oncology, or radiation oncology, or date of death.

### Statistical analysis

If not specifically stated on pathology reports, following assumptions were made at the time of data collection by each institution based on dermatopathology reporting conventions: 1. Tumor was considered well-differentiated if the pathology did not state it was poor or moderately differentiated; 2. Tumor depth of invasion was assumed to be in the dermis unless otherwise specified in the pathology/operative report; and 3. No PNI and LVI if not mentioned in the pathology report. The only remaining missing data were for tumor diameter (6%), which was imputed using the mode (10 mm), and age (0.2%), which was imputed using the mean (73.5 years).

Due to the characteristic differences between treatment arms, predictive modeling using truncated inverse probability of treatment weighting was performed to balance baseline patient/tumor characteristics.8 Propensity score represents the probability of receiving a treatment based on baseline characteristics. Probabilities were estimated for each tumor using a multinomial regression model that included all covariates listed in Supplementary Table II, available via Mendeley at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/p7jrtfdz4g/1. Each tumor was then assigned a weight (inverse probability of treatment weighting), with weights truncated at 0.01 for numerical stability.9 Weighted descriptive analyses were performed to confirm that baseline characteristics were balanced among the 3 treatment groups (Supplementary Table II, available via Mendeley at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/p7jrtfdz4g/1).

A weighted Fine and Gray competing risk modeling was performed for each outcome, with all-cause death as the competing risk for LR, NM, ITM, and DM, and non-CSCC death as the competing risk for DSD. As each outcome can occur separately in clinical practice, and the development of one outcome does not preclude the occurrence of another, each outcome was modeled independently. Each regression included the following patient and tumor risk factors as covariates: age at treatment (continuous numerical variable, bounding between 18 and 100 years), sex, immunosuppression (yes or no), histologic differentiation (well, moderate or poor), PNI (yes/no), LVI (yes/no), preoperative tumor diameter (continuous variable, capped at 30 mm), depth of invasion (dermis, subcutaneous fat, or beyond subcutaneous fat), anatomic location (head/neck or trunk/extremities), whether the tumor was recurrent at the time of inclusion into the cohort (yes/no; whereas LR was defined as a primary tumor within the dataset that ultimately recurred), and type of surgical treatment (Mohs/peripheral and deep en face margin assessment, WLE, or none). Covariate selection was performed a priori based on factors associated with CSCC recurrence.

Model performance was evaluated via 5-fold cross-validation with stratification by clinical site. Each site was randomly assigned to one of 5 testing folds so that patients from the same site were grouped in the same test set. This method was selected to evaluate the models’ capacity to generalize to new sites not included in the training split. The performance of riSCC, BWH, and AJCC8 was determined by the averaged truncated time-dependent C-Index accounting for ties, a discriminative measure quantifying the ranking agreement between predicted risk scores and observed event times where a value of 0.5 indicates chance performance and 1.0 indicates perfect performance, and Brier score, a calibration metric evaluating the alignment between predicted probabilities and observed event rates, across folds, evaluated at 3 and 5 years of follow-up.10 The performance in each of the cross-validation folds is also reported.

A final model (riSCC) was trained using all available data and used to estimate hazard ratios. All analyses were conducted using Python (Python Software Foundation) and R (R Development Core Team), employing the “riskRegression” library to implement the Fine-Gray models and “ipw” for inverse propensity weighting.9,11

Calibration curves (Fig 1) were generated to compare the predicted risk to the observed risk of experiencing outcomes within 5 years. A sliding window approach was employed across the riSCC predictions wherein the observed risk was calculated for all tumors that fell within a given window of predicted risk (window width of 5% in increments of 2.5% up to 20% for every increment for which there were at least 200 tumors). Within each window, the average predicted risk was calculated and plotted against the observed risk for all tumors within the window. The cross-validated predictions were used to generate the calibration plots (ie, the risk prediction for each tumor corresponded to when the tumor was in the testing split). Calibration was evaluated quantitatively using Brier scores (Supplementary Table III, available via Mendeley at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/p7jrtfdz4g/1).

### Development of application

The riSCC model was utilized to create a web-based and Apple/Android application. The website can be accessed at (https://riscc.scoutconsortium.org/) and applications will be available free of charge to download from the Apple App Store and Google Play.

## RESULTS

Twenty-three thousand one hundred sixty-six tumors from 12 sites were included in the cohort and utilized for analysis (Table II). Sixty-four percent (n = 14,811) of tumors occurred in males, and 20.4% were in immunosuppressed patients (n = 4725), with solid organ transplant (n = 2,007, 8.7%) being the most common reason for immunosuppression. There were 12,099 (52.2%) tumors on the head and neck. All tumors were staged according to the AJCC8 T staging system (regardless of tumor location), with 18,656 (80.5%) T1, 1860 (8.0%) T2, 2527 (10.9%) T3, and 123 (0.5%) T4a/b tumors. Using the BWH T Staging system, 17,247 (74.4%) were classified asT1, 3724 (16.1%) as T2a, 2016 (8.7%) as T2b, and 179 (0.8%) as T3. MMS/peripheral and deep en face margin assessment excision technique was used in 52.9% of tumors (n = 12,265), 31.7% of tumors were treated with standard excision (n = 7335), and 15.4% (n = 3566) of tumors were not surgically excised. Five hundred eighty-four tumors (2.5%) received postoperative adjuvant radiation (ART), and 90 tumors (0.4%) underwent postoperative adjuvant systemic therapy.

The median follow-up was 27.4 months (95% CI 0–102.8 months). A total of 742 (3.2%) LRs, 108 (0.5%) ITMs, 484 (2.1%) NMs, 150 (0.6%) DMs, and 308 (1.3%) DSDs occurred. Median time to occurrence was 7.8 months (95% CI 1.4–47.4) for LR, 7.6 (95% CI 0.8–35.6) for ITM, 7.9 (95% CI 0.7–39.9) for NM, 14.1 (95% CI 1.9–49.9) for DM, and 19.1 (95% CI 3.4–70.8) for DSD.

Table III outlines the results of the multivariable analysis with reported subdistribution hazard ratios for LR, ITM, NM, DM, and DSD. Risk of outcome occurrence with WLE was higher for all outcomes as compared to MMS/peripheral and deep en face margin assessment. The riSCC model demonstrated higher C-indices than AJCC8 and BWH T staging for all outcomes and time points (3 and 5 years) (Table IV). At 5 years, the mean C-indices for riSCC across cross-validation folds ranged from 0.74 for LR to 0.88 for ITM. Across the 5 folds and 5 outcomes (25 combinations), the performance of riSCC was higher than AJCC8 for 23 of 25 at 3 years and 24 of 25 at 5 years, and higher than BWH for 22 of 25 at 3 years and 23 of 25 at 5 years (Supplementary Tables IV and V, available via Mendeley at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/p7jrtfdz4g/1). Additionally, riSCC demonstrates the potential to stratify risk within T staging systems, as demonstrated by its subgroup C-index performance within stages (Supplementary Table VI and Fig 1, available via Mendeley at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/p7jrtfdz4g/1). The subgroup performance of riSCC was also consistent between immune intact and immunosuppressed patients (Supplementary Table VII, available via Mendeley at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/p7jrtfdz4g/1).

## DISCUSSION

Accurate risk prognostication is critical, yet challenging, for CSCC management given the heterogeneity of the disease and numerous factors that influence prognosis. riSCC offers improved prediction of CSCC outcomes compared to AJCC8 and BWH T staging systems. riSCC has been developed into a free web-based (https://riscc.scoutconsortium.org/) and downloadable application for iPhone and Android. The riSCC app takes less than 2 minutes to obtain personalized risk assessments for LR, NM, ITM, DM, and DSD for CSCCs treated with MMS and WLE.

Given the clinical significance, other studies have examined CSCC prognostication, including a published prognostic model from Rentroia–Pacheco et al in the Netherlands.5 While both this model and riSCC share several covariates, riSCC further incorporates surgical treatment, a factor that has been shown to impact recurrence, metastasis, and DSD (Manuscript In Press). Additionally, riSCC predicts 5 clinically relevant outcomes, as opposed to focusing solely on metastasis. The Netherlands model was developed using a nested case-control cohort derived from population-based European-only cohorts where most tumors are not treated with MMS, possibly limiting generalizability to the United States.12,13 Future studies comparing the prognostic models in various populations are needed, but was not feasible in our study, as we did not capture number of prior CSCCs, which the Netherlands model incorporates. More recently, molecular gene expression profile tests have also been developed to aid CSCC prognostication. Industry-sponsored studies have shown that gene expression profile enhances prognostication and may aid ART decision-making. Given the added cost, future studies are needed to evaluate how riSCC can help select tumors that may benefit from gene expression profile.14,15

Prognostication is also important to determine which tumors may warrant radiologic imaging.16 A study examining nodal ultrasound in 246 CSCCs found a 2.3% NM rate at baseline and on 6-month surveillance imaging in patients with primary CSCCs and negative clinical exams.17 However, approximately half the CSCCs were low-stage. When limiting analysis to recurrent CSCCs, metastasis increased to just over 10%. In contrast, 18% (n = 16) of 87 high-risk CSCCs developed NM. While radiologic imaging techniques are non-invasive, they involve additional costs, expose patients to radiation from several modalities, and require additional medical visits. As such, it is important to identify tumors at sufficiently high risk of poor outcomes to justify the use of radiologic staging and surveillance.

Accurate prognostication is important for therapeutic decision-making. While there is conflicting data on the efficacy of ART, one study of 508 high-stage CSCCs showed a 50% reduction in local and locoregional recurrence with ART.18–21 The National Comprehensive Cancer Network and American Society for Radiation Oncology guidelines include ART recommendations based on the presence of specific risk factors (extensive PNI, large or named nerve involvement, or if other poor prognostic features are present for National Comprehensive Cancer Network and gross PNI spread, recurrent tumors, AJCC8 T3 or T4 tumors, or desmoplastic/infiltrating tumors for American Society for Radiation Oncology).22,23 Identifying tumors with a high enough baseline risk to benefit from ART is important. Neoadjuvant cemiplimab for CSCC has over a 60% pathologic complete response or major pathologic response.24–26 The National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines recommend multidisciplinary consideration of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for rapidly growing tumors, in-transit metastasis, tumors with LVI, borderline resectable tumors, and cases where surgery alone may not be curative or result in significant functional limitation.22 If a prognostic tool can identify CSCCs with a high enough risk outside of these clinical scenarios, it may also be reasonable to consider treatment intensification.

Given the retrospective and multicenter nature of the study, the electronic medical records did not report features in the riSCC model for all tumors; however, the centers aligned on how to report missing variables. Additionally, treatment impacts CSCC outcomes but is not selected at random, and tumor differences, in part, likely influenced treatment selection. However, inverse probability of treatment weighting was utilized to balance potential differences in patient and tumor characteristics that impact treatment decision-making. riSCC has yet to be validated in an entirely unique cohort; however, a 5-fold cross-validation procedure stratified by hospitals was utilized to simulate validation across different clinical sites. Finally, riSCC output can aid in clinical decision making, but as with all risk stratification systems it is important to contextualize the results.

riSCC provides improved prognostication for CSCC, particularly for poor outcomes such as metastasis and death from disease, while also delivering a personalized risk assessment based on important clinical and histologic factors. The application is free to use, requires inputting 10 variables, and is designed for clinicians to use easily. Prospective validation studies of both the application and underlying model will be important next steps in assessing the utility of riSCC in clinical management.
